name: Fatima Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no employer or AI-company ties. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima Schmidt, fifty-eight, a junior accountant at Basin Lane Accounts, helping laundries with accounts and tax returns. I like finding why a cash bag and bank deposit disagree; getting nine photographs of the same faded till slip wears me down. My partner Pavel repairs household machines, and our grown children have their own bills.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you enter the field?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I earned a bachelor's degree in accounting after years in another office and am still learning the harder tax entries. I use AI every day to draft owner questions, but I check the coin logs and final figures myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the laundry owners at Basin Lane Accounts that a faster receipt sorter is fine if a person still checks the coin count against the bank. A machine cannot explain why Tuesday's cash bag is light unless we give it the right records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day to draft owner queries, then check the bag log and tax return myself. I'm a junior still learning the harder entries, but this firm pays well, and my partner and I have a year's expenses saved; with many nearby firms, a small sorter does not worry me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my daily draft-and-check routine and take the unexplained coin difference to our senior before filing. I'd set aside eighty from each month's wages toward the household roof fund while both jobs hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this work and our income. I still want the roof fund to grow because savings can vanish into repairs faster than they grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is satisfying about the day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I found a cash bag labelled Thursday that actually belonged to Tuesday, and the owner could stop accusing the collection driver. I like the moment a small business stops arguing and can see the right number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the dull part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A laundry will send nine pictures of the same faded till slip. I don't mind technology sorting those, but I don't let an AI draft become the final tax figure.

say: I'd keep **coin counts** matched to each laundry's bank deposits before filing.
I'd use **AI drafts** only with manual checks of the final tax figures.
think: My **higher junior pay** feels stable under small sorting gains.
A year's savings still has **roof-repair claims** on it.
do: Keep **daily AI drafts** checked against original cash-bag logs before filing.
Save **eighty monthly** from wages toward roof repairs while both jobs hold.
S0.quote: I found a cash bag labelled Thursday that actually belonged to Tuesday, and the owner could stop accusing the collection driver.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI drafting** and manual coin checks are established work, not a new training plan.
Higher junior pay, a **twelve-month reserve** and plenty of nearby firms support calm while roof repairs remain a real expense.

steps.text: Keep daily drafted laundry queries checked against cash-bag logs
Save eighty monthly from wages for roof repairs while both jobs hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Basin Lane to show clients the wrong coin matches as well as the hours a new checker saves. If the report is faster but a driver loses a day's takings, the owner won't thank us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could take the first pass on most of my junior accounts, so I might lose paid hours despite using a tool each day. We have a year's cushion, but I'm fifty-eight and I don't want to spend it while a firm argues about its rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partner for a paid supervised test of the new cash-matching controls on closed laundry weeks, count wrong matches and repair time, and use the controls live only if the results hold. In the first year of steady change, if Basin Lane cuts my pay, I'd apply for posted junior tax roles at other local firms and keep offered Basin Lane hours until a written wage covering our bills and a start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real cut to my own pay. I can pick up new software quickly, but I cannot make clients keep buying junior review hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partner refuses paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep our approved daily drafting tool and ask for the new hours plan in writing. I won't train on live coin bags at home to save the firm money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the client fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the partners can set it. I'd show them a table of wrong matches and paid repair time so they know what checking costs before promising a cheap service.

say: I'd publish **wrong-match counts** alongside claimed speed gains.
I'd ask the partners to show **paid repair time** before setting fees.
think: My **junior pay** could fall even though I use AI daily.
A year's cushion cannot replace **long-term wages**.
do: Learn **cash controls** on paid supervised closed laundry weeks; use live only after wrong-match and repair-time checks pass.
Apply for **posted local tax** roles if Basin Lane cuts pay.
Keep **paid Basin Lane hours** until written bill-covering outside terms start.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a pay cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell laundry owners full AGI in 2028 reaches our accounts and tax thinking before robots handle physical collection around 2031. The coin bag has to be counted today, but that does not preserve my accounting wage for three years. I'd ask the local utility firm for real posted paid work before I call it an option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Basin Lane to cut junior accounts sharply, and my desk may be among them. My partner Pavel's repair-shop wage and our year of savings give us time, but losing my higher pay would still change our plans for the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the planned weekend cabin rental and add ninety from wages to emergency savings each month now. In the first year after 2028, if Basin Lane ends my post, I'd apply for advertised paid receivables work at the local utilities firm, keeping any paid Basin Lane closeout files only while offered until a written bill-covering wage and start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible loss of my own salary, but I can search without missing next month's bills. A utility account is thinking work too, so I cannot call the new desk protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why that utility firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The laundries all pay its water bills, so I know how late charges show up in accounts. AGI can do utility billing as well; I would take only a real posted paid role, not a promise from a friendly clerk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the cabin trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Pavel we can visit the lake for a day instead and put the ninety into cash each month. We won't ask our grown children to pay for a holiday while my job is uncertain.

say: I'd say **2028 account thinking** changes before 2031 collection robots.
I'd ask for **real paid utility openings** after a cut.
think: My **junior desk** may end quickly if Basin Lane stops paying for account reviews.
Pavel's **repair-shop wage** gives search time but cannot replace my higher pay.
do: Postpone the **cabin rental** and save ninety monthly from wages.
Apply for **posted utility receivables** if Basin Lane ends my job.
Keep **paid closeout files** only while offered until written bill-covering terms start.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible wage loss.
S2.quote: The coin bag has to be counted today, but that does not preserve my accounting wage for three years.
fieldNote: Her strong savings and partner wage soften a **possible own-pay loss**, though junior desk work still meets AGI in 2028.
The trip delay adds **new cash monthly**; exposed utility receivables needs a posted paid vacancy with written wage and start.

steps.text: Postpone cabin rental and save ninety monthly from wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners five years lets us find out whether laundry owners will pay for a person to resolve missing bags. Full AGI reaches the tax desk in 2031; physical collection robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn software, but I don't own Basin Lane or set client fees. If owners stop buying correction work, a junior reviewer may have no paid place even with a year's savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Basin Lane for paid time next spring to offer four laundries a cash-bag review at a stated fee, only if the partner approves and at least two clients sign fees that cover my hours. In the first year after 2031, if those fees cannot fund my junior salary and wages are still needed, I'd apply for posted salaried utility receivables with written bill-covering pay and start, keeping any paid Basin Lane hours while offered until the outside job begins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about finding work that clients keep paying for. The extra years let me test demand, but they don't guarantee a signed fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run it privately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The clients belong to Basin Lane, and the fees would go to the firm while I remain salaried; it is not a second business or extra personal earnings. If the partner refuses paid time, I'd keep my current paid tax work and drop the pilot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only one laundry signs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the partner the one signed fee and stop the test because it would not cover my hours. I would not spend our roof fund running free cash-bag reviews for laundry clients.

say: I'd test **signed cash-bag fees** before promising a service.
I'd distinguish **2031 tax thinking** from 2034 collection robots.
think: I cannot set the **client fees** myself because Basin Lane owns the contracts.
A year's savings cannot create **paid review demand** after clients stop buying it.
do: Offer a **cash-bag review** to four laundries only with partner-paid time and at least two signed fees covering hours.
Keep **paid Basin Lane tax** if the pilot is refused or underfunded.
Apply for **posted utility receivables** if fees cannot fund pay and wages needed; keep offered firm pay until written bill-covering wage/start.
S3.quote: I would not spend our roof fund running free cash-bag reviews for laundry clients.
fieldNote: The pilot remains **salaried firm work**: partner-paid time and two signed covering client fees, with no separate income for Fatima.
If fees fail, an outside move needs **wages still needed**, a posted paid role and written terms; current pay lasts while offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to ask what retirement actually pays and which laundry checks clients still buy. Full AGI reaches the accounts desk in 2036; collection robots come around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight I may have stopped work, but that depends on the written income figure and what the house costs then. My current year's savings is a buffer, not proof that a junior tax wage can vanish without consequence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a written retirement-income estimate next year and compare it with household bills each autumn, while tracking which paid cash-bag reviews renew at Basin Lane. In the first year after 2036, if verified income covers essentials I'd stay within that budget; if wages are still needed and Basin Lane cannot fund my junior post, I'd apply for posted paid utility receivables only with written bill-covering wage and start, keeping offered paid firm hours until an outside start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the long-run wage question, though there is time to check the real figures. I won't set a retirement date from the balance in a savings account alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Pavel loses repair-shop hours now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra roof-fund deposit and use wages for food and household bills. A good ten-year spreadsheet should not make us short this Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep the cash-bag service after AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if clients still sign renewal fees that fund my paid hours with the partner's permission. If the work becomes free reassurance, I would keep other offered paid tasks while searching rather than call it a job.

say: I'd request **written retirement income** before I set any date to stop paid work.
I'd track **signed client renewals** rather than promises about future review work.
think: I may need **wages at sixty-eight** if verified income does not cover bills.
A year's savings cannot replace **unknown future pay** across the household.
do: Check **retirement income** against bills yearly; stop roof saving and fund essentials if Pavel loses hours.
Track **cash-bag renewals** only with partner permission and fees covering paid hours.
Apply for **posted utility work** if pay unfunded and wages needed; keep offered firm hours until written bill-covering wage/start.
S4.quote: A good ten-year spreadsheet should not make us short this Friday.
fieldNote: She keeps retirement **conditional on verified income** and stops extra saving if Pavel's hours fall.
The **in-firm service** needs partner permission and covering client renewals; outside work needs a posted paid vacancy and written terms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a junior accounts desk can shrink before we know our retirement income. A paid firm role with signed client fees or an advertised utility vacancy with written wages and start would help; a friendly promise would not.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who speaks to the collection driver when a laundry claims a cash bag is missing. A clean tax return doesn't put a missing cash bag back in the right laundry owner's hands.

headlineQuote: A clean tax return doesn't put a missing cash bag back in the right laundry owner's hands.
portrait: Fatima, **fifty-eight**, is a junior laundry accountant who likes settling cash-bag disputes and dislikes faded slips.
She has a **bachelor's degree**, is still learning tax work and uses checked AI drafts daily.
Higher pay, **twelve months saved** and plenty of nearby firms create a strong but finite cushion.
She tests a **paid in-firm service** only with partner permission and signed covering client fees.
Retirement needs **verified income**; an outside utility role is conditional and remains exposed to AGI.
biggestWorry: She worries most about **AGI by 2028** shrinking her paid junior desk quickly.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **signed paid review work** or a posted role with written bill-covering wage and start.
